text: — Dravichkata, gentlemen, tells stories so well that after him it is difficult to satisfy you with any story. And to tell you the truth, I also know some things about Bai Ganyo — Vasil spoke up. — From Moscow, from Petersburg!
— Get on with it already, stop beating around the bush! — Dravichka replied to him.
— The word "twisted" doesn't seem particularly poetic to me — Mato joked.
— Quiet, gentlemen. Vasil! Come on, my dear, start!

— On the way to Petersburg — Vasil began — we stopped at the station in Vilno. We were traveling together as a pair — Bay Ganyo and I. We went into the buffet. Bay Ganyo wanted me to treat him, since I had been smoking his tobacco along the way. I ordered beer and a snack. The buffet manager listened in on our conversation, recognized, it seemed, that I was Bulgarian, and asked us in Russian: — Excuse me, gentlemen, I believe you are Bulgarians?
We answered him affirmatively.
— Do you know Mr. Dimitrov, the student?
— I don't know him, do you know him, Bay Ganyo!
— Dimitrova? Wait... aha! I remember. Dimitrov, I know, I know him. A sharp boy, I know him, of course!
— Can't you tell me where he is now? — asked the innkeeper.
— He is in Constantinople now — replied Bai Ganyo, — in a week he will be getting married there. He's struck a bargain!
— Ho-ow! — the innkeeper cried out as if thunderstruck. — He’s going to get mar-ried? But he was married here, gentlemen!...
— Of course. Look, ha, ha, ha! — Bay Ganyo chuckled heartily. The innkeeper looked at him in wonder.
— You don't know him — continued Bay Ganyo, turning to me, — he's an awfully sharp kid, that Dimitrov...

The innkeeper told us the following: “One day, gentlemen, Mr. Dimitrov arrived by rail with a deaf-mute 13–14-year-old boy. I had known Dimitrov from a year earlier; he lived in our town, fell in love with a girl, they got married and left for Moscow or Petersburg—I don't know. When he came this year with the deaf-mute boy, he told me that this boy had a brother in your country, in Bulgaria, an official or an officer—I don't remember—who was going to send him a hundred francs monthly so that he could live in one of the Petersburg institutes for the deaf and mute. Since Mr. Dimitrov was leaving for some other city—at least that's what he told me—he asked me to take the boy into my home, to feed him, to look after him until his arrival. He assured me that he would return after ten days or so. I agreed, took in the unfortunate child, and looked after him as my own. Ten days passed, a month passed, two passed, and not a word was heard from Dimitrov. I want to find out something from the child—he is deaf-mute, poor thing, he cannot tell me. And, I see, that child grew sad. I wrote to Petersburg, to Moscow—no one replied. In the third month, gentlemen, the boy disappeared. We asked, we searched, we reported to the police, we sent telegrams in several directions—nothing, the poor child was gone. What became of that child, I still do not know. Let Mr. Dimitrov bear the sin for it, I will bear a loss of 100 rubles... So you say that he is to be married next Sunday? My God, how is such a thing possible? For God's sake, gentlemen, report this to your superiors, warn this unfortunate girl he is going to marry...”

I promised the innkeeper that as soon as I reached Petersburg, I would inform a gentleman who, I was certain, would immediately telegraph the Exarchate. I settled my bill. We boarded the train and set off for Petersburg.
— You just had to interfere — Bai Ganyo said to me reproachfully, — how do you know what kind of person his wife here is.

We were traveling in third class. Bay Ganyo took up two seats and lay down to take a nap. At the next station, several more passengers entered our carriage and the extra seats had to be yielded to them, but Bay Ganyo is no fool — he pretends to be asleep and snores and snores. A giant German, a peasant, approached Bay Ganyo with a bag in hand and began to wake him by gently nudging his boots. Bay Ganyo keeps quiet and just lets out a hrr... puff... hrr... puff... and having covered his face from the German, he winks at me, as if to say "look at how sly I am." "Now, get up!" the German shouted and began to poke my companion quite noticeably. Hrrr... puff!... "Now, don't pretend, you devil!" the German growled and with one sweep brushed away Bay Ganyo's legs, sent him tumbling over his saddlebags, and sat down with us. Bay Ganyo pretended to be startled, rubbed his eyes and immediately, as if nothing had happened, took out his cigarette case and offered it open to the German: — Bulgarian tobacco!
— Ah, so you are Bulgarians! Very nice to meet you — the German said good-naturedly and began to roll himself a cigarette. — You are going to Piter. And I am too. Together, then.

As soon as we reached Petersburg, I hastened to fulfill my promise made to the innkeeper in Vilno. I met with my acquaintance and recounted to him Dimitrov’s escapade. He immediately telegraphed to Tsarigrad and succeeded in stopping the impending wedding. He, for his part, told me the rest of the story regarding the deaf-mute boy. When and how he had been coached to flee from Vilno is not known, but one day he arrived in Petersburg, and here for a long time he was the victim of the basest exploitation by Dimitrov, who not only pocketed the sums sent by the unfortunate boy’s brother but also forced the poor child to go from door to door to all the most influential figures and well-known philanthropists in Petersburg to beg for money. And not only in Petersburg, but he often pushed him as far as Kronstadt, to the famous saint of the common folk, John of Kronstadt...
I, having almost no means of subsistence, was forced to live in the Deshovka, a refuge for extremely poor students. Bay Ganyo most energetically insisted that he too should come to the Deshovka.
— But it's not possible, Bay Ganyo, this establishment is only for students.
— So what if it's for students — Bay Ganyo was trying to convince me — aren't students people like me? What's the harm, after all, in taking in a Bulgarian?
— But you are a rich man, Bay Ganyo, you can pay for a hotel.

— What a simple man you are — Bay Ganyo reproached me, — I thought you were craftier. Hey there, Bulgarian, why should we give our money to the Muscovites? If you come across a windfall, hold it with both hands, indeed! How would they know what my situation is?
— It's not possible, Bay Ganyo; the poor students will protest, they will be angry with me, and they might kick me out of the dormitory.

— Stubborn Bulgarian head! — Bay Ganyo continued. — Don't you have a mouth? Don't you have enough wits to tell them that I'm your brother, that I'm a man in need; why, it's enough just to say that I'm Bulgarian, you know the Russians, what fools they are!...
— No, no, I can't! — I cried out resolutely and started towards Deshovka.

— Aha! You think you'll get rid of me that easily! Wait! You haven't seen anything yet! — mutters Bay Ganyo and walks after me. — A Bulgarian! And this is supposed to be a Bulgarian! Not a penny's worth of patriotism!... Wait, man, don't hurry so much, I can't catch up with you, my saddlebags are heavy! Wait, Bulgarian!...

At that moment we presented, it seemed, a rather curious sight, for the people passing on the sidewalks turned and looked at us intently. Bay Ganyo was ten paces behind me, his saddlebags slung over his shoulder on his cane, his rug draped over his other arm, which he raised every now and then to wipe his sweaty brow. His fur cap was barely clinging to the crown of his head. Bay Ganyo strode after me, grumbling: "Wait, for God's sake, man, at least take the rug, it’s pulling my arm off... You think you can shake me off! You don't know what a piece of work your Bay Ganyo is!..." I walked awkwardly, calculating in my mind how I would show up with Bay Ganyo at the Deshovka and how I would justify this impulsive act. I’ll have to lie! And I see that shaking him off is unthinkable! Finally, since it was only for a few days, I reluctantly resigned myself to the situation. And Bay Ganyo kept walking and walking behind me, still grumbling, but he dropped his tough-guy talk and began in a minor key: "Listen here, Bay Vasil, wait a bit, I beg you, Bay Vasil, we’re Bulgarians, after all..."

And imagine, gentlemen, at that moment I felt sorry for Bay Ganyo! Believe me! I realized that his action was outrageous, that he was a disgusting miser, an egoist, a cunning trickster, a hypocritical exploiter, a brute and a boor to the marrow of his bones... but I felt sorry for him: in the subtle vibrations of the tone with which he spoke those last words, my ear caught a tender note that had been hidden and remains hidden in Bay Ganyo's heart, but rarely—God, how rarely!—does it appear... I do not know, it may seem funny to you, unnatural, but I will tell you, gentlemen, that at that moment I looked at Bay Ganyo differently; as if someone suggested to me: "Do not despise this simple, cunning, dear wretch; he is a child of a crude environment, he is a victim of crude educators; the evil does not reside in him himself, but in the influence of the surrounding environment. Bay Ganyo is active, sensible, receptive—mainly receptive! Place him under the influence of a good leader, and you will see what feats he is capable of performing. Bay Ganyo has so far manifested only his animal energy, but within him lies a great store of potential spiritual power, which awaits only a moral impulse to be transformed into a living force..."

We arrived at the Deshovka. Most of the students had not yet returned from vacation, so there were plenty of vacant places. My bed had been saved by my faithful comrade Kocho, an Albanian, a pauper in the highest degree, who received three rubles a month from the Slavic Society for tea and sugar; he had entered the university and studied there for two years, but having convinced himself that it was not for him, he left it and entered the seminary. This Kocho was good, he would give his head for a friend, but God forbid you irritate him—in an instant all his Arnaut passions boil over, as he turns pale, turns green, his eyes fill with blood, a total beast!... When I entered the room with Bay Ganyo, we found Kocho in a horizontal position on the bed: on this bed it was difficult to determine at once which was the pillow, which the bedding, which the coverlet... Kocho jumped from his bed with the lightness of a panther, hugged me, kissed me, met Bay Ganyo and, cheerful, grinning from ear to ear with joy, arranged for us to sit, one on the bed, another on a trunk, while apologizing for the slight disorder in the room. Then he opened the door and let out an Arnaut cry: "Vanka, put on the samovar, my dear fellow!" — "What do you need a samovar for, when there is no tea and sugar!" — the dear fellow called out from the end of the corridor. Kocho grabbed his head with both hands, strode across the room, snatched his hat and, without hearing our pleas to stay, saying that we would buy tea and sugar, tore himself away, shouted "right away" and disappeared... Bay Ganyo and I waited half an hour, we waited a whole hour—Kocho did not return. Something must have happened to him.

In order not to waste the beautiful day, I suggested to Bay Ganyo that we go out for a walk. “Hey, wait, let’s wait a bit, the man will treat us to tea,” Bay Ganyo objected; he could not let a freebie pass, no matter where it came from. But still, I insisted on my way. Bay Ganyo shoved the vials into his sash and we went out. As we were approaching Anichkov Bridge, we heard from afar a beastly cry, mixed with the most desperate curses and insults; we stepped onto the bridge and what did we see!... Kocho, enraged like a tiger, had dug his iron fingers into the neck of an unknown gentleman, whose hat was rolling on the stones, had bent his head down and was straining to throw him off the bridge. The victim was making every effort to escape, but it was not so easy to tear himself away from the hands of the frenzied Arnaut. “Charlatan!” roared Kocho. “Scoundrel! Villain! You are the spy, not me, you are the spy, you son of a bitch! I will kill you, you vile creature!” I rushed to pull them apart. Bay Ganyo shouted after me: “Leave them be, man, why do you need trouble on your head, let them break their heads; leave them, they’ll drag you as a witness through the police stations.” I did not heed Bay Ganyo’s advice and headed toward the Arnaut, who did not stop tearing his throat and spewing the most shameful epithets at his victim, whom he had already dragged to the edge of the bridge, and, it seemed to me, one more moment—and the stranger would fly headfirst into the clear waters of the Fontanka. “Charlatan! Scoundrel!” roared Kocho, digging his bony fingers even more tightly into his opponent’s thick neck.

When I was already a few steps away from them, the victim, startled by the impending doom, made a desperate move, tore himself from the hands of the Albanian, instantly grabbed his soiled hat, and bolted. “Stop, charlatan! Filthy coward, scoundrel!” Kocho grabbed a stone and threw it after him. The stranger ran to a tram, hopped inside, and disappeared... But the Arnaut did not calm down: “I will kill you, vile charlatan!” — he continued to growl, gesturing with his fist toward the space where his enemy had vanished. I called Kocho by name; he turned and did not recognize me!... In his gaze, there was something beastly, his eyes shone, his face had turned green and dark, his teeth chattered as if in the strongest fever, his lips trembled convulsively and let out a hollow growl. “W... w... b... r... r... Charrll... Bit... t... s... scoundrel... m... m... m... Charlatan!” — he shouted once more, turning with a threat toward the invisible enemy. “Kocho, my dear, what happened to you, who is this gentleman?” — I asked with friendly sympathy. He fixed his eyes on me and looked at me senselessly and maliciously, and again he did not recognize me!... “I will kill you, vile creature! I will show you who is a spy!” — Kocho growled and threatened the passing tram, as if his enemy were sitting in every single tram.

"Kocho, please, tell me what happened to you — I implored my friend, who was driven to madness with rage. — Who was that gentleman?" Kocho looked at me once more and shouted: "That man is the greatest scoundrel! Do you understand? The grea-test scoun-drel!" — and again he turned his eyes away, and again he set about spewing curses. I began to suspect that my friend was the victim of some villainy concocted by his enemy, but exactly what it was, I did not figure out and could not have figured out. What Kocho told me was so base that it could not even be a subject of guesswork.

We managed to calm Kocho down somewhat and went with him into a tavern to drink tea. We lingered here for quite a long time, engrossed in the Albanian's stories about Aslanova's humiliating escapades. Even Bay Ganyo did not dare to shout his "bravo!" or "ashkolsun!"; on the contrary, from time to time he clicked his tongue, shook his head in wonder, and said: "My, what a complete ass this man was!" We left the tavern and set off along Nevsky Prospect. A mixed crowd from all parts of the world filled the sidewalks of the brilliant street; we could barely maneuver between the passers-by. All sorts of carriages moved along the street in two rows. Shops, each more magnificent than the last, enticed the eyes of the public. Bay Ganyo deigned to express the opinion that "after all, Petersburg isn't such a bad place either"... For a whole hour we pushed through the crowd until we reached the Neva. As soon as we came out onto the quieter English Embankment, we hadn't even managed to take ten steps when Kocho pulled me abruptly by the sleeve and cried out in a choked voice: — There he is!
— Who?
— The charlatan!
— Which charlatan?

— The Greatest! Stop! Let's hide so he doesn't notice us! — he muttered and dragged us by the sleeves behind the columns of a gate. Bay Ganyo poked his nose out from behind the column and looked in the direction indicated by Kocho.
— Who do you see? — asks Kocho.
— I see a man — whispers Bay Ganyo mysteriously. — Say, Vasil, take a look, this man looks a lot like our Dondukov-Korsakov.
— He is the same — replies Kocho, — who else do you see?

— I see two more people, kneeling before Dondukov, look! Tsk... tsk... tsk... they are kissing his boots, crying, begging him for something, beating their chests, look! Tsk... tsk... tsk... he wants to shake them off, but they won't let him go — one from this side, the other from that, embracing his legs...
— Look closely, can't you recognize any of them? — the Albanian dictated.

— I can't, how will I recognize them, they are constantly rattling their heads in his boots... Ha, wait — said Bay Ganyo — wait!... I recognized him! Why, he... it's true! Why, he's that one, the one you were going to throw off the bridge... it's him!
— He is the same... the scoundrel! You are now witnesses to one of his wretched comedies! — growled the Arnaut through clenched teeth. — Come on, let's slip back onto "Nevsky Prospect" now.
— Wait until we see the end of the scene — I stated.

— It is not necessary — said Kocho decisively, — the end is known: they will hold him by the legs and cry until he gives them a few rubles or some recommendation to another victim, or some intercession... These scoundrels are capable of disgracing the name of an entire nation...
— My! This fellow was a total donkey — exclaimed Bay Ganyo and clicked his tongue.
— Well, why did you stop, Vasil? Keep going! — one of the group called out.
— Tell me about the story with Ermolova...
— Leave it, I'm disgusted — Vasil stated.
— Or for Princess Belozerskaya...
— Leave it, I can't anymore!
— And do you know the story of Bai Ganyo and the tripe soup? — another one chimes in.
— Well, do you know anything about the shaved mustaches...

— Enough, gentlemen! Bay Ganyo's stories are endless. Let's start the second part of the gathering already. Marcus Aurelius, sing something, my little dove! Or you, Kalina-Malina, sing a little something!... Come on: "Roll u-u-up, Velo girl, white sleeve-e-es...."
The second part of the party began... After midnight we dispersed.

Goodbye, Bai Ganyo! Travel around Europe, spread to all corners the product of our beautiful Rose Valley and... I beg of you, Bai Ganyo, look a bit deeper into European life, may you see its face, enough of this wretched reverse side forcing itself upon you!...
